title: Going a Woman’s Way
note: What desire brings isn’t enmity outright, but it wrecks gain and brings ruin, so it is counted with enmity. First comes a man following the way of his wife, who should be following his.

couplets.plain: Men who dote on their wives won’t win the finest reward. Men who are set on action want no part of that.
couplets.pm: Men who crave their wives for pleasure and take on their ways won’t gain righteousness, their sweet companion. Men bent on making wealth scorn that pleasure as an obstacle. It keeps them from the righteousness she makes possible, and from wealth, which serves both righteousness and pleasure. So it must be given up.
couplets.sensitive: Treats devotion to a wife as a lure away from greatness

links.quote: Men who dote on their wives
links.reason: Sets doting on a wife against any hope of the finest reward.

links.quote: Men who are set on action
links.reason: Speaks to men as husbands, and says those set on action want no part of this.

couplets.plain: The gains of a man who craves a woman, careless of all else, become a great disgrace and bring him shame.
couplets.pm: The wealth of a man who gives up his manhood and craves his wife’s womanhood brings great shame on all men, and shame on him too. He can’t make wealth, so it has merely come to him. She takes its fruits, giving and enjoying, so the manly part is now hers. All men are ashamed, and seeing his lack of manhood, he is ashamed in the end too.
couplets.sensitive: Holds a man's love for his wife up to public shame

links.reason: Even his gains become a great disgrace once he craves a woman, careless of all else.

couplets.plain: The unnatural habit of bowing to your wife will always bring you shame among good people.
couplets.pm: A man’s fear, which makes him bow to his wife, always brings him shame when he goes among good men who lack it. It is her nature to live in fear, so his fearing her goes against nature. Since he fears her, no one is left to keep her in order, and every fault follows. So he says “always”.
couplets.sensitive: Treats deferring to a wife as shameful weakness

links.quote: always bring you shame among good people
links.reason: Bowing to his wife brings a man shame among good people.

couplets.plain: A man who fears his wife has nothing for the next life, and his skill at work wins him no glory.
couplets.pm: A man who lives in fear of his wife has no reward in the next life. Even if he can manage his work, good people won’t celebrate it. He lacks the goodness that household life needs, so he has no next life. Without a nature of his own he can’t carry his work through, so it brings no glory.
couplets.sensitive: Scorns a man who fears his wife; could reach an abused husband

links.quote: A man who fears his wife

couplets.plain: A man who fears his wife will always be afraid to do good to good people.
couplets.pm: A man who fears his wife is always afraid to do good to good people, even with wealth he earned himself. Good people are the gods, great ascetics, the worthy, his parents and good guests. Doing good means giving them what they want. “Always” means even on the days it must be done.
couplets.sensitive: Blames a frightened husband; could reach someone abused at home

links.quote: afraid to do good to good people
links.reason: Fear of his wife reaches outward and stops him doing good even to good people.

couplets.plain: Though they live like the unblinking gods, men who fear their wives’ bamboo shoulders have no standing.
couplets.pm: Men who fear their wives’ bamboo shoulders may live on earth like the gods who won heaven by valour, yet they have no manhood. That means being honoured for beating the shoulders of hostile warriors, which can’t really happen. “Bamboo shoulders” shows how slight the cause of fear is. Though they beat warriors’ shoulders, men who fear hers aren’t men.
couplets.sensitive: Shames men for being in awe of their wives

links.quote: men who fear their wives’ bamboo shoulders have no standing
links.reason: Living like the gods earns nothing for men who fear their wives’ shoulders.

couplets.plain: A woman with modesty has more greatness than the manhood of a man who lives at a woman’s bidding.
couplets.pm: The manhood of a man who, without shame, goes about doing his wife’s bidding is lower than her womanhood, with its modesty. “With modesty” isn’t needed for her, but it stresses his lack of shame in serving her. She has the distinction of getting him to do her bidding.
couplets.sensitive: Treats a woman's lead as beneath a man's dignity

links.quote: A woman with modesty has more greatness
links.reason: Ranks such a man’s manhood below the greatness of a woman with modesty.

couplets.plain: Men who live as a fair-browed woman wishes won’t meet their friends’ needs and won’t do good.
couplets.pm: Men who live as their wives want, not as they themselves want, can’t meet the needs of friends, and can’t do the righteousness that helps them in the next life. “Fair-browed”, like “bamboo shoulders”, shows how slight the cause is. She can’t know of these needs herself, direct him or give out wealth, so nothing needed for either life gets done.
couplets.sensitive: Blames a wife's influence for a man's failures

links.quote: won’t meet their friends’ needs and won’t do good

couplets.plain: Righteous acts, great wealth and other deeds are not found in those who do a woman’s bidding.
couplets.pm: Righteous action, the wealth-making that carries it out, and the other acts, those of pleasure, aren’t found in men who do their wives’ bidding. There are five senses, so those acts are many. Men who gave up the first two for these pleasures find that she now has the upper hand, so even the pleasures are lost.
couplets.sensitive: Says a wife's direction empties a man's life of all good

links.quote: those who do a woman’s bidding
links.reason: Holds that nothing worth having survives in a man who does a woman’s bidding.

links.quote: Righteous acts, great wealth and other deeds
links.reason: Counts what such a man loses: righteous acts, wealth and other deeds, the aims of life.

couplets.plain: Those with a broad, thinking heart never have the folly that comes of clinging to a woman.
couplets.pm: Rulers whose hearts are given to planning their work, and who have the wealth that comes of it, never have the folly born of clinging to a wife, even in youth. That folly is the cause of the three faults above: craving her, fearing her and doing her bidding. So he sums up all three here.
couplets.note: இடன் usually means breadth or room. He reads it as wealth.
couplets.sensitive: Calls a man's devotion to his wife folly

links.quote: the folly that comes of clinging to a woman
links.reason: Claims those with a broad, thinking heart never give way to this, and calls it folly.
